The post US$144m savings boost for Barbados appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Barbados has secured more than US$144 million in fiscal savings through innovative debtfor- nature and debt-forclimate transactions, creating financial room for major investments in water security, sewage modernisation, coastal resilience and protection of the island’s marine ecosystems.

Donna Wellington, chief country and commercial officer at CIBC Caribbean, said the Barbados transactions demonstrated how financial innovation could simultaneously strengthen a country’s fiscal position and create room for sustainable development.

The bank has been involved in the climate and conservation financing, while across its Caribbean markets it has arranged or invested about US$820 million in sustainable finance initiatives.

It has also financed more than 213 megawatts of clean energy assets across the Caribbean and Central America, including renewable energy projects in Curaçao, Jamaica, the Cayman Islands and elsewhere.

Wellington said such investments were about more than simply financing individual projects.

The transactions were among a series of major Caribbean infrastructure and sustainable finance investments highlighted at the tenth Caribbean Infrastructure Forum (CARIF) in Miami last week, where regional financial leaders examined how the region can attract more private capital to fund its development needs.

“These projects demonstrate a simple but powerful truth: strategic infrastructure investment delivers returns that multiply. It attracts private capital, creates jobs, improves productivity, builds resilience, and strengthens national competitiveness,”said Wellington.

CIBC Caribbean has led or arranged more than US$1.5 billion in infrastructure transactions over the past decade, supporting ports, airports, hospitals and other critical infrastructure across its regional markets.

The investments come as Caribbean governments face growing demands for infrastructure capable of withstanding climate change while improving energy security, water supplies, transportation and public services.

The forum, now in its tenth year, brought together banking, development finance and advisory leaders to examine how governments and project developers can turn those needs into projects capable of attracting financing.

(PR/NS))

The post Browne: Potential was enormous appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
A three-year effort to hand ownership of Barbados’ sugar industry over to its workers has collapsed.

Chairman of CoopEnergy Barbados, Lieutenant Colonel Trevor Browne, announced late Friday night that Government had withdrawn from signed contractual agreements. However, he said not all hope was lost from their end.

“It was devastating, to be quite honest,” he told the Sunday Sun yesterday.

“The potential for good here was enormous, for the enfranchisement of ordinary people, for making people feel proud, for changing a traditionally questionable whole plantation system. That was revolutionary in terms of the vision we had, so it was very disappointing. And the more we got involved, the more doable it appeared. So obviously, we’ve been very disappointed.”

In a statement to sugar workers and the public, CoopEnergy said the Government’s exit ends a divestment plan that would have transferred the Agricultural Business Company Limited (ABC) – previously the Barbados Agricultural Management Company (BAMC) – operations into joint private ownership between CoopEnergy and the sector’s own sugar workers, an arrangement the company had hoped would turn labourers into shareholders, owners and directors of the industry that employs them.

When contacted yesterday, Minister of Agriculture, Food and Nutritional Security Dr Shantal Munro-Knight revealed that chairman of the ABC, Ambassador Dr Clyde Mascoll, was out of the island.

“I am attempting to get details on the matter. I am only now seeing the press release (from CoopEnergy) in the last hour,” she said, opting not to comment any further.

According to CoopEnergy, the divestment was originally driven by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan conditionality tied to Barbados’ economic reforms. It said BAMC had for decades cost taxpayers roughly $20 million a year in subsidies to prop up an industry beset by longstanding problems.

Working alongside BAMC leadership, CoopEnergy said it built a divestment plan that won full Government endorsement, first through a memorandum of understanding (MOU) and later through shareholders’ and subscription agreements creating two new companies, ABC and the Barbados Energy and Sugar Company (BESCO). Those agreements were approved by Cabinet and signed on December 18, 2023, alongside the IMF’s loan approval, the entity pointed out.

Then, CoopEnergy added, communication largely stopped. It said public and private pressure mounted for it to “bring money to the table”, even as BAMC withheld the financial records and asset registry the signed agreements required it to hand over. Other cooperative organisations approached separately for funding were met with the same unmet request, according to the statement.

Matters came to a head on August 18, 2025, when CoopEnergy received its first formal notice that BAMC intended to “vitiate” the shareholder agreements for both companies immediately. CoopEnergy said it objected, noting the contracts contained no provision for unilateral termination and instead required disputes to go through mediation. It said BAMC agreed, and mediation ran from March to August of this year, but ended without agreement or any sign further talks would help.

However, in a paid advertisement last November, BAMC had contended that the confidentiality of the MOU was breached and it was “unfortunate” the terms were made public.

“Instead of resolving issues privately between the parties, public statements were made that caused doubt and anxiety regarding the partnership and the viability of the industry,” BAMC listed as a concern.

It noted the need to protect the interests of former employees who were promised shares and “the failure to complete the intended investments may have created uncertainty for staff, farmers, suppliers and other stakeholders”.

In March of last year, Browne had raised concerns about stalled negotiations as well as changes to the original agreement and said CoopEnergy would not be buying a pig in a bag.

“It would be irresponsible for any cooperative in Barbados to authorise such significant investments in an industry that has been known to be failing, without complete financial disclosure, as well as coherent business projections, which clearly show how previous failings are to be addressed,” he said then.

Then Minister of Agriculture Indar Weir, in turn, said CoopEnergy had been making excuses for not investing the agreed $16 million.

“I cannot continue to take excuses about the injection of funds they were supposed to have done since the inception. To drag this out by using things like not receiving financial statements . . . and to use their delay to suggest there is a stalemate,” he said.

The initial payment was $4 million and Weir said if CoopEnergy was unable to meet its financial obligations, another entity would do so.

Asked where the sugar industry goes from here, Browne said that question was no longer CoopEnergy’s to answer.

“We have a clear vision of where we would like to make it go, and we offered it, and we were willing to do that, but essentially, it was not accepted.”

Pressed on a way forward, he added: “We don’t have a plan in mind; hopefully things will work out.”

Browne said he remains unable to account for the reversal.

“The strange thing is that we don’t really understand why it didn’t work out. Everybody was on board initially. Then suddenly, that changed, without any explanation to us. We still don’t understand why.”

Despite the breakdown, Browne said CoopEnergy has not closed the door.

“We are so committed to this project that if there is an opportunity for us to get involved again, we definitely will.” (BA)

item.content:encoded:
Dennis de Peiza has demitted the office of General Secretary of the Congress of Trade Unions and Staff Associations of Barbados after 24 years.

Yesterday it was announced in a press release that his departure had taken effect from Thursday. de Peiza did not seek reelection at the recently concluded 31st Biennial Delegates Conference of the Congress.

In his address to the Business Session of the Conference, he reminded delegates and observers of his journey within the organisation.

He said that with the establishment of CTUSAB in 1995, he was elected as the first treasurer, thereafter graduated to the office of Assistant General Secretary and then to General Secretary; the office in which he has served unchallenged for the past 24 years. de Peiza expressed gratitude to the member organisations of CTUSAB for having repeatedly restored their confidence, trust and faith in him to lead and manage the organisation. His parting advice to fellow trade union leaders, to recognise the value of teamwork within organisations.

He gave the assurance as a committed servant, who has worked tirelessly as a volunteer during his working life as a teacher, and even in the time of his retirement, of his continued commitment and support to the congress and to the cause of labour. ( PR)

The post Six juveniles charged with multiple offences appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Six juveniles have been arrested and formally charged with a series of offences, including robbery, endangering life, use of a firearm and theft of motor vehicles.

The charges stem from incidents reported between February and September 2026 and were laid by the Barbados Police Service Major Crime Unit and Criminal Investigations Department in Hastings/Worthing, Central, Black Rock and District ‘A’.

Among the charges are multiple counts of robbery, endangering life, use of a firearm, wounding with intent and theft of motor vehicles.

The juveniles also face charges including aggravated burglary, assault with intent to rob, assaulting police officers, resisting a police officer and escaping lawful custody.

Four of the juveniles appeared before Magistrate (Ag) Jared Richards in the District ‘A’ Traffic Court on Thursday, while the other two appeared before Chief Magistrate Douglas Frederick on Wednesday.

They were not required to plead to the indictable offences.

One juvenile was granted $2,000 bail, while the other five were remanded to the Barbados Prison Service at Dodds.

All six are scheduled to reappear in court on October 15.

The OAS said the initiative was launched this week during its first consultation mission to Antigua and Barbuda, marking the beginning […]

The post OAS to support Antigua and Barbuda in strengthening democratic participation in schools appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
The Organisation of American States (OAS) will collaborate with the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology of Antigua and Barbuda to strengthen democratic participation, responsible citizenship and youth engagement within the country’s education system.

The OAS said the initiative was launched this week during its first consultation mission to Antigua and Barbuda, marking the beginning of the project.

The September 15-16 mission was led by OAS Education Specialist Cecilia Martins and brought together curriculum development experts, policymakers, education professionals, students and other stakeholders.

Minister of Education, Science and Technology Daryll Matthew said the initiative reflects the government’s commitment to creating learning environments where students develop the knowledge, skills and values needed for active and informed citizenship.

The technical assistance is being coordinated by the OAS Department of Human Development, Education and Employment (DHDEE), under the Directorate of Education and Culture of the OAS Executive Secretariat for Integral Development, through the Democratic Education and Citizenship Programme (DEMEP).

The OAS said DEMEP brings together 29 member states and promotes implementation of Article 16 of the Inter-American Democratic Charter, which recognises education as an important means of strengthening democratic institutions, developing human potential and alleviating poverty.

The initiative, funded by the United States, will support a review of existing policies, curricula and initiatives and help identify priorities for future training and tool development.

The OAS said the experience will also contribute to the exchange of best practices through the Inter-American Committee on Education and related follow-up mechanisms. (CMC)

item.content:encoded:
CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets.

An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and a security guard confiscated them, the outlet reported.

CNN also said Saturday morning that one of its reporters was denied access and had her badge seized.

Trump said on Friday he was barring MS NOW, CNN, and Politico – three major US media outlets – from the White House, accusing them of writing “fiction or lies” about his administration. Press freedom advocates called the move “unconstitutional”. (BBC News)

item.content:encoded:
Three men have been charged in connection with two alleged robberies earlier this month, including an incident on September 12 during which a serious bodily harm charge was also laid.

Nathan Caleb Barker, 22, of Citrus Drive, Workmans, St George; Akeem Kareem Inniss, 23, of Bonwell Road, St Joseph; and Racaid Akeil Leroy Holder, 34, of Orange Grove, St Joseph, were arrested and formally charged by the Criminal Investigations Department (South).

All three face joint charges of using a firearm, robbery and causing serious bodily harm stemming from September 12.

Inniss and Holder are also jointly charged with using a firearm and robbery in connection with an incident on September 11.

Inniss faces additional charges of driving without insurance, driving without a licence, driving without reasonable consideration, driving without due care and attention, and failing to comply with a beacon and siren. Those offences also relate to September 12.

The three men are scheduled to appear in the District ‘A’ Criminal Court today, September 19.

item.title: Bajans nudged to embrace 60 and 5 events
item.dc:creator: Josue Ramirez Nelson
item.description:
Barbadians at home and abroad were yesterday encouraged to partake in the varied planned events as the country celebrates its 60th anniversary of Independence and fifth anniversary as a republic. Attorney General and chair of the celebrations committee, Wilfred Abrahams, gave the rallying call during a press conference at Ilaro Court, held to launch the […]

The post Bajans nudged to embrace 60 and 5 events appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Barbadians at home and abroad were yesterday encouraged to partake in the varied planned events as the country celebrates its 60th anniversary of Independence and fifth anniversary as a republic.

Attorney General and chair of the celebrations committee, Wilfred Abrahams, gave the rallying call during a press conference at Ilaro Court, held to launch the National Calendar of Independence celebrations.

Abrahams noted that Barbadians can expect a full programme of national activities that cater to the history, culture and community of the country.

“We want Barbadians of every age and in every community to feel that there is a place for them in this celebration. So much of our progress began with ordinary people determined to give their children a better life. Their achievement belongs to all of us. Barbados at 60 and five [as a republic] will embrace the whole of our story, including the painful chapters of enslavement and struggle,” he said.

The calendar of events will feature a number of campaigns such as Let Me Paint Barbados and the National Clean It Campaign where communities were invited to beautify their spaces.

Culture

Meanwhile the Bridging the Gap lecture series, historical commemorations, the Food and Rum Festival, and the NIFCA Gala will inject a dose of culture and heritage into the mix.

There will also be traditional showcases such as the lighting ceremony, along with the Independence and Republic Concert, the National Ceremonial Parade, the presentation of national honours, the Spirit of the Nation show and the National Service of Thanksgiving.

Additionally, through My Voice, My Barbados, primary, secondary and tertiary students will be able to share their ideas and vision for the country in an oratory competition.

Rounding out the ambitious celebrations will be the Prime Minister’s Football Cup Finals which will spotlight the women’s division for the first time since its inception three years ago.

Abrahams highlighted that these were not solely a Government event and welcomed businesses, churches and communities to add celebrations of their own to the occasion.

“This is your calendar. There’s more than enough room for your events. We welcome schools, businesses, churches and community organisations to bring their own activities forward. Your creativity can help make this celebration feel at home in every parish.

“We also want to encourage a personal promise to Barbados . . . your very own pledge to this nation that we love. It could be teaching a young person a skill, spending time with an elderly neighbour or starting a family habit that brings everyone closer.

“Show something that you know you can do, that you know you can follow through with and invite somebody else to join you. This moment gives us a chance to renew our pride in this country and our commitment to one another. We can carry this spirit into the way we care for our surroundings, keep our promises and use our talents to make life better,“ he added.

Alongside the presentation of National Independence Honours, this year will see the Barbados Diamond Anniversary Honours established to commemorate the diamond jubilee celebrations.

Cabinet secretary Selma Green explained that the honour is bestowed upon citizens who have shown exceptional service and achievement and contributed significantly to national development and nation building. Persons who already hold a national honour or decoration are not eligible.

Green appealed for Barbadians to recognise those who have shown the qualities befitting the honours both at home and abroad.

“Somewhere in Barbados and somewhere in our diaspora is a person who has given years of service without seeking recognition, whose contribution has transformed lives and whose example reflects the very best of who we are. You may know that person.

“Let us ensure that in this historic year, those who have helped Barbados move upward and onwards know that their country sees them, values them and is grateful for their service,” she added.

Nominations for both the National Independence Honours and the Barbados Diamond Anniversary Honours will close on Friday, September 25.

(JRN)

item.title: PM to appoint special group
item.dc:creator: Barry Alleyne
item.description:
Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley yesterday announced she will appoint a special committee of historians and economists to build a Barbadosspecific case for reparations, telling delegates at the third CARICOM Reparations Conference that the region’s moral argument must now be matched by hard evidence, even as she insisted the political will to act remains the […]

The post PM to appoint special group appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley yesterday announced she will appoint a special committee of historians and economists to build a Barbadosspecific case for reparations, telling delegates at the third CARICOM Reparations Conference that the region’s moral argument must now be matched by hard evidence, even as she insisted the political will to act remains the ultimate test.

Speaking at the Wyndham Sam Lord’s Castle Resort in St Philip, on the opening day of the conference, Mottley said the committee would be tasked with quantifying the specific historical and economic harms Barbados had experienced from the transatlantic slave trade, moving beyond broad moral appeals.

“I will be appointing a technical committee of historians and economists to do the research so that our business-specific case can quantify the kinds of things that we have seen and experienced in this region,” she said, adding that other CARICOM member states should do the same.

The prime minister, drawing on her own background as a lawyer, said the credibility of the region’s case depends on the strength of its documentation.

“If your evidence is not strong, then you cause a disorder or a referral to the opposition,” she told delegates, arguing the Caribbean must shift from being “advocates for the movement” to becoming “advocates for the case.”

She said the principle “where there is a will, there is a way” applies as much to the work ahead in Barbados as it does to the wider global movement, describing sustained political will, not further delay, as the real obstacle to justice.

Mottley pointed to Barbados’ legislative history as proof that reparatory action is possible recalling that the Barbados parliament passed the 1661 Slave Code, which she said became “the blueprint for how other countries and colonies framed their understanding of what black people were”, as chattel, but later found the will to repeal the 1830 Consolidated Slave Act after the Colonial Office deemed it “so offensive” that it forced the law’s withdrawal in 1831.

Right to purchase

She also cited the 1980 Tenantries Freehold Purchase Act, which gave families who had lived for generations on plantation lands the right to purchase that land, as the country’s “first national act of reparations”. Mottley framed access to land, rather than education, as the more urgent unfinished struggle in Barbados’ post-slavery history, noting the country had already built 200 primary schools by 1900.

The forthcoming committee, she suggested, would build on that by producing the kind of rigorous, quantified case needed to press claims internationally. She drew a comparison to Holocaust reparations to illustrate what she sees as a double standard: “Since 1952, the Germans have paid $95 billion to the Jewish community as a result of a Holocaust of six years,” she said, stressing that no one seeks to diminish that history, but that a system of enslavement lasting 211 years, by her accounting, from Barbados’ 1627 settlement, had produced no comparable reckoning.

Mottley also linked the domestic committee’s work to her broader critique of global financial hypocrisy, arguing that wealthy nations lecture indebted countries on fiscal discipline while engaging in massive money-printing themselves calling it “the germ of hypocrisy”.

Beyond the committee, Mottley proposed a global petition campaign running five to six months to build public pressure alongside government diplomacy, building on a UN resolution she said had already won backing from 123 countries. She credited former US President Barack Obama for his continued engagement with the cause.

She closed by urging that indigenous peoples be included in the reparatory justice conversation, citing the Garifuna’s expulsion from St. Vincent and the dispossession of indigenous communities in Guyana, Suriname and Belize.

“There is never going to be a right time to have this discussion,” Mottley said. “We are not boulders, we are not monsters, we do not bear arms, we have come to have a conversation.” (BA)

item.title: Caddle: FSC gets more power
item.dc:creator: Shawn Cumberbatch
item.description:
The Financial Services Commission(FSC) is being given more power to supervise and regulate the non-bank sector. The House of Assembly on Tuesday debated and approved the Financial Services Commission (Amendment and Validation) Bill, 2026, which not only validates the charging and collection of fees by the FSC “over a certain period”, but strengthens that agency’s […]

The post Caddle: FSC gets more power appeared first on nationnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
The Financial Services Commission(FSC) is being given more power to supervise and regulate the non-bank sector.

The House of Assembly on Tuesday debated and approved the Financial Services Commission (Amendment and Validation) Bill, 2026, which not only validates the charging and collection of fees by the FSC “over a certain period”, but strengthens that agency’s ability to do its job.

The legislation was piloted by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office with responsibility for Economic Affairs and Planning Marsha Caddle, who linked the amendments passed partly to the FSC’s signing of memoranda of understanding (MOU) with the International Organisation of Securities Commission (IOSCO) and International Association of Insurance Supervisors.

Both MOUs relate to cooperation and the exchange of information, the minister said. “This Bill and these proposed amendments seek not just to validate the fees that have recently been collected over previous years, or the collection of those fees, but it seeks to continue to modernise and to strengthen the legislative framework that governs the Financial Services Commission,” Caddle said.

“We have sought to amend the legislation to enhance the supervisory and the regulatory powers of the FSC to allow it to gather information and exchange information, and also to engage in international regulatory cooperation, sharing information with other institutions in other countries.”

The Member of Parliament for St Michael South Central added that the IOSCO MOU “serves to set an international benchmark for cross-border cooperation. It provides regulators of securities like the FSC with the kinds of tools that we need to be able to fight cross-border fraud and misconduct that can weaken global markets and undermine investor confidence”.

She added: “One of the things that this will allow Barbados to do is to make sure that we remain competitive, we remain marketable to investors and potential investors and other companies, especially when it comes to things like compliance and mutual assistance.

“But also that we are able to create a domestic environment where people who do business here feel safe in the execution of that business and are able to see their companies grow in the ways in which such companies might grow in other countries.”

She also said the MOUs and legislative amendments will put the FSC in a better position to protect consumers in an environment where financial instruments continued to evolve.

“We have seen a lot in the [cryptocurrency] space and in that market . . . we have, quite frankly, seen quite a few actors who have not been on good footing to operate, and in several jurisdictions this has had tremendous costs to individuals, because there are people who seek to invest in new ways,” she told the House.

“People will hear you could get a return of eight and nine per cent [up to] 15 per cent. That sounds like magic. And so they take up the money that they’ve been saving for retirement, that they’ve been saving to make sure that their child is able to go to university, and they’ve put it at the disposal of some company that is selling a new product.

“That is not to say that a new product or service is always nefarious. In fact, in most cases, it is not. But to be able to share information from jurisdictions that have already started regulating, that means that Barbados and others will be able to get ahead of the curve a bit.” (SC)
